# Desargues Involution Theorem and Isoconjugations

## Desargues Involution Theorem

:::{#thm-desarguesInvolutionTheorem}
## Desargues involution theorem, DIT
Let $A,B,C,D$ be four points on the conic $\mathcal{C}$, and let $\ell$ be a line not passing through $A,B,C,D$. Suppose that $\ell$ intersects $\mathcal{C}$ at points $X,Y$, then
$$
(X,Y),\,(AB\cap \ell,CD\cap \ell),\, (AC\cap\ell,BD\cap \ell),\, (AD\cap\ell, BC\cap\ell)
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that
$$
(X,Y;\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap AC)\stackrel{A}{=}(X,Y;B,C)_{\mathcal{C}}\stackrel{D}{=}(X,Y;\ell\cap DB,\ell\cap DC)=(Y,X;\ell\cap DC,\ell\cap DB)
$$
This shows that $(X,Y),(\ell\cap AB,\ell\cap CD),(\ell\cap AC,\ell\cap BD)$ is an involution. The same argument applies for the fourth pair.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
From DIT, given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through $A,B,C,D$, the map
$$
g:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell,\,X\mapsto\ell\cap (ABCDX)
$$
(where $\ell\cap (ABCDX)$ denotes the second intersection of $\ell$ and $(ABCDX)$) is an involution. From this viewpoint, it is natural to regard $\mathbb{P}_{AB}\cup\mathbb{P}_{CD}$ as a conic.
:::

:::{#cor-tangentConicsDit}
Given points $A,B,C,D$ (no three of which are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through any of them, there are exactly two conics passing through $A,B,C,D$ and tangent to $\ell$ (the tangency points are the fixed points of the involution).
:::

:::{#thm-ddit}
## DDIT
Let $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in\mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ be tangent to a conic $\mathcal{C}$. Set $\ell_i\cap \ell_j=A_{ij}$ for $1\leq i<j\leq 4$. Suppose that $P$ is not on $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4$, and $m,n$ are the two tangents to $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $P$, then 
$$
(m,n),(PA_{12},PA_{34}),(PA_{13},PA_{24}),(PA_{14},PA_{23})
$$
is an involution.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This is the dual of Desargues involution theorem.
:::

In Desargues involution theorem, the points $A,B,C,D$ need not be distinct, and a line becomes a tangent when they coincide. Dually, in DDIT, if two lines coincide, their intersection becomes the tangency point.

:::{#thm-carnot}
## Carnot theorem
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $A_1,A_2\in BC,\,B_1,B_2\in CA,\,C_1,C_2\in AB$. Fix point $P$ not on the three sides, then there exists a conic $\mathcal{C}$ intersecting the three sides of $ABC$ at $A_1,A_2,B_1,B_2,C_1,C_2$ if and only if
$$
\prod_{i=1}^2 A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^2 B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot  \prod_{i=1}^2 C(A,B;P,C_i)=1
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that such a conic $\mathcal{C}$ exists, then we apply DIT to the quadrangle $B_1C_1B_2C_2\in\mathcal{C}$ and line $BC$,
$$
(A_1,A_2),(B,C),(B_1C_1\cap BC,B_2C_2\cap BC)
$$
is an involution, i.e.
$$
(B,C;B_1C_1\cap BC,A_1)\cdot (B,C;B_2C_2\cap BC,A_2)=1
$$
However, $(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot A(B,C;P,B_iC_i\cap BC)^{-1}$, from Menelaus theorem,
$$
(B,C;B_iC_i\cap BC,A_i)=-A(B,C;P,A_i)\cdot B(C,A;P,B_i)\cdot C(A,B;P,C_i)
$$
for $i=1,2$. Multiplying these for $i=1,2$ yields Carnot theorem.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The equality in Carnot theorem is equivalent to the existence of an isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ such that
$$
\varphi(AA_1)=AA_2,\,\varphi(BB_1)=BB_2,\,\varphi(CC_1)=CC_2
$$
We may take $\varphi$ to be the $(BB_1\cap CC_1,BB_2\cap CC_2)$-isoconjugation.
:::

From Carnot theorem and Ceva theorem, the vertices of two cevian triangles are conconic.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $P_aP_bP_c$ and $Q_aQ_bQ_c$ be the cevian triangles of points $P$ and $Q$ with respect to $ABC$, then the points
$$
P_a,\,P_b,\,P_c,\,Q_a,\,Q_b,\,Q_c
$$
are conconic. This conic is called the **Carnot conic** (or **Cevian conic**) of $P$ and $Q$. The Carnot conic of $P$ and $P$ (which is tangent to the three sides of $ABC$ at the vertices of the cevian triangle of $P$) is called the **inconic** of $P$ (with respect to $ABC$). The $P$-anticomplement of the inconic of $P$ is called the **circumconic** of $P$ (i.e. the conic tangent to the three sides of the anticevian triangle at $A,B,C$).
:::

## Isoconjugations and Circumconics


In @thm-isoconjugate, we defined the $(P,Q)$-isoconjugation $\varphi$, denoted $\varphi=P\times Q$.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. All points on side $BC$ (except for $B,C$) are sent to $A$ by $\varphi$, and $\varphi(A)$ is the entire line $BC$. This suggests that we should not consider the image of the vertices $A,B,C$ under isoconjugations when there is no additional structure (for instance, some lines or conics passing through the vertices).
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. A line $\ell$ passing through $A$ is sent to a line $\varphi(\ell)$ passing through $A$ by $\varphi$ (omitting the image of $A$ itself). We use the convention that $A\in \ell$ is sent to $\varphi(\ell)\cap BC\in \varphi(\ell)$ by $\varphi$. On the other hand, if a conic $\mathcal{C}$ passes through $A$, let $\ell$ be the tangent of $A$ to $\mathcal{C}$, and we use the convention that $A\in \mathcal{C}$ is sent to $\varphi(\ell)\cap BC\in\varphi(\mathcal{C})$ by $\varphi$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that the tripolar of $P$ and $\varphi(P)$ are $\ell$ and $m$, respectively, then $\varphi(AP)=A\varphi(P)$. From harmonicity, $\varphi(A(\ell\cap BC))=A(m\cap BC)$.
:::

:::{#lem-isoconjline}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that the tripolar of point $P$ is $\ell$, the circumconic of $\varphi(P)$ is $\mathcal{C}$, then 
$$\varphi(\ell)=\mathcal{C},\,\varphi(\mathcal{C})=\ell$$
and $\varphi:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to \mathcal{C}$ is a projective map.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $X$ is on $\ell$, then
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_B\to \mathbb{L}_C,\,B\varphi(X)\mapsto BX\mapsto X\mapsto CX\mapsto C\varphi(X)
$$
is projective. By Steiner conic, the locus of $\varphi(X)=B\varphi(X)\cap C\varphi(X)$ is a conic $\mathcal{C}'$ through $B,C$. Similarly, $\mathcal{C}'$ is a circumconic (i.e. a conic passing through the three vertices). Let the tripolar of $\varphi(P)$ be $m$, then the tangent of $C$ to $\mathcal{C}'$ is
$$
f(BC)=\varphi(C(\ell\cap AB))=C(m\cap AB)
$$
Note that this is the tangent of $C$ to $\mathcal{C}$, so we similarly see that $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{C}'=\varphi(\ell)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let $\varphi=P\times P$. Suppose that $\ell$ is the tripolar of $P$, then $\varphi(\ell)$ is the circumconic of $P$.
:::

We may similarly prove the following example by Steiner conic.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
A conic $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $B$, $C$ (but not through $A$) is sent to a conic through $B,C$ by an isoconjugation.
:::

:::{#lem-trilineardual}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$, and let $P,Q$ be points not on the sides of $ABC$. The following statements are equivalent.

(1) $P$ is on the circumconic of $Q$.

(2) $Q$ is on the tripolar of $P$.

(3) $\varphi(Q)$ is on the circumconic of $\varphi(P)$.

(4) $\varphi(P)$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(Q)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $P$ is on the circumconic of $Q$. Let $P_aP_bP_c$ and $Q_aQ_bQ_c$ be the cevian triangles of $P$ and $Q$, respectively, then the tripolar of $P$ passes through the harmonic conjugate $P_b'$ of $P_b$ with respect to $A|C$ and the harmonic conjugate $P_c'$ of $P_c$ with respect to $A|B$. Consider the projective map
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_{AC}\to \mathbb{L}_{AB},\,P_b'\mapsto P_b\mapsto P\mapsto P_c\mapsto P_c'
$$
Since $f(A)=A,\,f(C)=Q_c,\,f(B)=Q_b$, the tripolar $P_b'P_c'$ of $P$ passes through a fixed point $Q$ as $P$ varies.

This shows that (1)$\implies$(2) and (3)$\implies$(4). From @lem-isoconjline, (2)$\implies$(3) and (4)$\implies$(1).
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Given an isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$, $P$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(Q)$ if and only if $Q$ is on the tripolar of $\varphi(P)$. This may be regarded as the tripolar version of La Hire theorem. Define $\mathfrak{p}(X)$ to be the tripolar of $\varphi(X)$, then $\mathfrak{p}$ is a dual transformation such that $\mathfrak{p}^2$ is the identity, so $\mathfrak{p}$ is indeed a polar transformation by @polarequiv.
:::

:::{#lem-isoquadrilateral}
Let $\varphi=X\times X'=Y\times Y'$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then 
$$
\varphi(XY\cap X'Y')= XY'\cap X'Y
$$
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $XY\cap X'Y'=Z$, $XY'\cap X'Y=Z'$. Apply DDIT to the quadrilateral formed by lines $XY,X'Y',XY',X'Y$ and point $A$,
$$
(AX,AX'),(AY,AY'),(AZ,AZ')
$$
is an involution. A similar argument on the vertices $B$ and $C$ shows that $\varphi(Z)=Z'$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
In @lem-isoquadrilateral, if $A,X,Y$ are collinear, then $X\varphi(Y)\cap Y\varphi(X)$ is on $BC$.
:::

:::{#lem-isoconconic}
Let $\varphi$ be an isoconjugation on $ABC$. Suppose that $P,Q$ are points such that line $PQ$ does not pass through $A,B,C$, then 
$$
A,\,B,\,C,\,P,\,Q,\,P\varphi(Q)\cap Q\varphi(P)
$$
are conconic.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Note that $\varphi(P),\,\varphi(Q),\,PQ\cap\varphi(P)\varphi(Q)$ are collinear. From @lem-isoconjline and @lem-isoquadrilateral, $A,\,B,\,C,\,P,\,Q,\,P\varphi(Q)\cap Q\varphi(P)$ are conconic by applying $\varphi$.
:::

:::{#lem-fixed-points-isoconjugation}
Suppose that $\varphi=P\times P$ is an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then $\varphi(X)=X$ if and only if $X$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $\varphi$ maps $AX$ to $AX$,
$$
A(B,C;P,X)=A(C,B;P,X)=A(B,C;X,P)
$$
We see that $A,X,P$ are collinear or $A(B,C;P,X)=-1$. Similarly, $X$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$.
:::

The following lemma is a special case of @lem-isoconconic.

:::{#lem-tangent-conic-isoconjugation}
Suppose that $\varphi=P\times P$ is an isoconjugation on $ABC$, then line $P\varphi(X)$ is tangent to $(ABCPX)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $P\varphi(X)$ intersect $(ABCPX)$ again at $Y$. Applying $\varphi$, $P\varphi(X)$ is sent to $(ABCPX)$, so $\varphi(Y)=Y$. From @lem-fixed-points-isoconjugation, $Y$ is equal to $P$ or one of the vertices of the anticevian triangle of $P$, but the latter are not on $(ABCPX)$, so $Y=P$.
:::

## The Fixed Points of an Isoconjugation and Desargues Involution Theorem

:::{#lem-isoconjugatefix}
An isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ has exactly $4$ fixed points, that is, there are four points $P$ satisfying $\varphi(P)=P$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Since $BX\mapsto B\varphi(X)$ is an involution, there are two fixed lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$. A similar argument on the vertex $C$ gives two fixed lines $m_1,m_2$, then the fixed points are precisely the four intersections $\ell_i\cap m_j$, $i,j=1,2$.
:::

This shows that isoconjugation is uniquely determined by the four fixed points: the cevian triangle of the four fixed points is the triangle where the isoconjugation is defined.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $P,Q,R,S$ be four points (no three of which are collinear) such that the cevian triangle of $PQRS$ is $ABC$. Define the isoconjugation of the complete quadrangle $PQRS$ to be the isoconjugation $\varphi$ on $ABC$ such that $\varphi(P)=P$.
:::

:::{#thm-quadrangle-isoconjugation}
Let $\varphi$ be the isoconjugation of the complete quadrangle $PQRS$. For any conic $\mathcal{C}$ passing through $P,Q,R,S$, $X$ and $\varphi(X)$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\ell=X\varphi(X)$, and let $\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}$ intersect at points $U,V$. We apply DIT to the quadrangle $PQRS$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and the line $\ell$,
$$
(U,V),(\ell\cap PQ,\ell\cap RS), (\ell\cap PR,\ell\cap QS),(\ell\cap PS,\ell\cap QR)
$$
is an involution. Let $ABC$ be the cevian triangle of $P$ with respect to $QRS$, then from the definition of isoconjugation,
$$
-1=A(X,\varphi(X);P,R)=(X,\varphi(X);PQ\cap \ell,RS\cap\ell)
$$
This shows that the harmonic conjugation with respect to $X|\varphi(X)$ sends $PQ\cap \ell$ to $RS\cap\ell$, and similarly, we see that the involution we obtained from DIT is the harmonic conjugation with respect to $X|\varphi(X)$, i.e. $(X,\varphi(X);U,V)=-1$. We conclude that $X$ and $\varphi(X)$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::{#lem-eight-point-conic}
Suppose that the anticevian triangles of points $P,Q$ are $P_AP_BP_C$ and $Q_AQ_BQ_C$, respectively, then
$$
P,\,P_A,\,P_B,\,P_C,\,Q,\,Q_A,\,Q_B,\,Q_C
$$
are conconic. We call this conic the **eight-point conic** of $P,Q$ (with respect to $ABC$).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $\mathcal{G}=(PP_AP_BP_CQ)$. Triangle $ABC$ is self-conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{G}$, so $A,AQ\cap BC$ are conjugate with respect to $\mathcal{G}$. Note that
$$
(A,AQ\cap BC;Q,Q_A)=-1
$$
Since $Q$ is on $\mathcal{G}$, $Q_A$ is also on $\mathcal{G}$ by La Hire theorem. Similarly the eight points are conconic on $\mathcal{G}$.
:::

In other words, if two complete quadrangles share the same cevian triangles, then the eight vertices are conconic. Sometimes, the eight-point conic may degenerate into two lines.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
We say that isoconjugations $\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\varphi_3$ on $ABC$ are collinear if for all $X$, the points $\varphi_1(X),\varphi_2(X),\varphi_3(X)$ are collinear.
:::

:::{#lem-isoconjugateline}
The isoconjugations $\varphi_i$ are collinear ($i=1,2,3$) if and only if there exists a point $X$ such that $X_i=\varphi_i(X)$ are collinear ($i=1,2,3$).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Take the eight-point conic passing through the fixed points of the isoconjugations $\varphi_1,\varphi_2$, then from @thm-quadrangle-isoconjugation, the polar of $X$ with respect to $\mathcal{G}$ is $X_1X_2$. Since $X_3\in X_1X_2$, the fixed points of $\varphi_3$ are on $\mathcal{G}$. Given point $Y$, then $Y_1,\,Y_2,\,Y_3$ are collinear on the polar of $Y$ with respect to $\mathcal{G}$.
:::

We may directly prove @lem-isoconjugateline: given $Y$, $(X\div Y)\times X_i=Y_i$, and $X\div Y$ is a projective transformation.

:::{#cor-diagonalconic}
Consider the family of isoconjugations $\varphi$ such that $\varphi,\varphi_1,\varphi_2$ are collinear, then the fixed points of all $\varphi$ lie on a fixed conic $\mathcal{G}$, and for all $X\in \mathbb{P}$, $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(X)= \varphi_1(X)\varphi_2(X)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Given a point $P$ and a line $\ell$, $P\times X$ are collinear for all $X\in \ell$. Denote by $P\times \ell$ the collection of all such $P\times X$. From @cor-diagonalconic, $P\times \ell$ may be regarded as a polar transformation (such that the polar of $P$ is $\ell$ and $ABC$ is self-conjugate).
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
In @lem-trilineardual (and the subsequent remark), given an isoconjugation $\varphi=P\times Q$, there exists a conic $\mathcal{G}$ such that the tripole of $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(X)$ is $\varphi(X)$. Let the tripolar of $Q$ be $\ell$, then $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}(P)=\ell$. This shows that $P\times \ell=\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}$, i.e. the conic associated to the isoconjugation $P\times Q$ and the conic defining $P\times \ell$ are both $\mathcal{G}$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Consider the dual of isoconjugations: let $ABC$ be a triangle and $\ell_1,\ell_2$ be two lines. Let $f_A$ be the involution $(B,C),\,(\ell_1\cap BC,\ell_2\cap BC)$, and define $f_B,f_C$ analogously; define the **line-isoconjugation** $\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}=\ell_1\times \ell_2$ such that for each line $m$, $\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}(m)$ is a line passing through $f_A(m\cap BC),\,f_B(m\cap CA),\,f_C(m\cap AB)$.
:::

Let the tripole of $\ell_1,\ell_2,m$ be $P_1,P_2,Q$. Define $\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}=\ell_1\times \ell_2$, $\varphi=P_1\times P_2$, then the tripole of $\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}(m)$ is $\varphi(Q)$. This shows that line-isoconjugations and isoconjugations are in one-one correspondence by tripoles/tripolars. The conics defining $\varphi^{\mathbb{L}}$ and $\varphi$ are both $\mathcal{G}$, where $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{G}=P_1\times \ell_2=P_2\times \ell_1$.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The isoconjugations defined in @thm-isoconjugate should be called "point-isoconjugations", denoted by $\varphi^\mathbb{P}$. For historical reasons, isoconjugations mean point-isoconjugations by default.
:::

## The Circular Points of Infinity

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Define $\infty_+$ and $\infty_-$ to be the **circular points of infinity** (i.e. any two distinct points in $\mathbb{P}$). The line $\infty_+\infty_-$ is called the **line at infinity**, denoted $\ell_\infty$. For a line $\ell\neq\ell_\infty$, the **point at infinity** on $\ell$ is $\ell\cap\ell_\infty$, denoted by $\infty_{\ell}$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
The purpose of defining the circular points of infinity is to introduce some classical objects, such as circles and angles. When we assign two points to be the circular points of infinity, some projective statements become well-known lemmata.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Suppose that $\infty_\ell=\infty_m$, then lines $\ell,m$ are said to be **parallel**, denoted $\ell\parallel m$.
Define the **midpoint** of $A$ and $B$ to be the harmonic conjugate of $\infty_{AB}$ with respect to $A|B$. The **center** of a conic $\mathcal{C}$ is defined to be $\mathfrak{p}_\mathcal{C}(\ell_\infty)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
The **angle** between lines $\ell_1,\ell_2\neq\ell_\infty$ ($\ell_1,\ell_2$ shall not pass through $\infty_{\pm}$) is
$$
\sangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)=(\infty_{\ell_1},\infty_{\ell_2};\infty_+,\infty_-)
$$
For three points $A,B,C$, define $\sangle BAC=\sangle(BA,AC)$. By definition, 
$$
\sangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\sangle(\ell_1,\ell)\cdot\sangle (\ell,\ell_2)
$$
If $\sangle (\ell_1,\ell_2)=-1$, the lines $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ are said to be **perpendicular**, denoted $\ell_1\perp\ell_2$. Define $\infty_\ell^{\perp}$ to be the harmonic conjugate of $\infty_\ell$ with respect to $\infty_+|\infty_-$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
If we define $\measuredangle BAC=\dfrac1{2i}\log\sangle BAC$, then
$$
\measuredangle(\ell_1,\ell_2)=\measuredangle(\ell_1,\ell)+\measuredangle (\ell,\ell_2)
$$
If $\ell_1\perp\ell_2$, then $\measuredangle (\ell_1,\ell_2)=\dfrac1{2i}\log e^{\pi i}=\dfrac\pi2$, which coincides with the usual definition of directed angles. From this definition, if two directed angles differ by an integer multiple of $\pi$, then they are the same, for $e^{2\pi i}=1$. This suggests that directed angles and the $\sangle$ defined here are essentially the same, except that addition is replaced with multiplication.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
A conic $\omega$ is said to be a **circle** if $\omega$ passes through $\infty_+$ and $\infty_-$. The conic $(ABC\infty_+\infty_-)$ is the only conic passing through the vertices of $ABC$, called the **circumcircle** of $ABC$, denoted $\odot(ABC)$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
To make sure the objects are well-defined, when it comes to circumcircles or angles, all lines are assumed not to pass through the circular points of infinity.
:::

:::{#cor-concyclic}
The points $A,B,C,D$ are concyclic if and only if $\sangle ACB=\sangle ADB$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
A triangle $ABC$ is said to be $A$-isosceles if $\sangle ABC=\sangle BCA$.
:::

:::{#lem-isosceles-circle}
Let $O$ be the center of the circle $\omega$. Suppose that $A,B$ are points on $\omega$, then $OAB$ is $O$-isosceles.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let $AO,BO$ intersect $\omega$ again at $A',B'$. Consider the involution with perspector $O$, then (note that $O\infty_\pm$ is tangent to $\omega$)
$$
(A',B;\infty_+,\infty_-)_\omega=(A,B';\infty_+,\infty_-)_\omega
$$
i.e. $\sangle A'AB=\sangle ABB'$. We conclude that $OAB$ is $O$-isosceles.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
This is essentially the property that all points on a circle are equidistant to its center, but we are not defining lengths for now.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Define the **isogonal conjugation** on $ABC$ to be $\varphi=\infty_+\times \infty_-$. The term "isogonal" comes from the equality $\sangle BAX=\sangle \varphi(X)AC$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $ABC$ be a triangle. The definition of some points is symmetric with respect to the three vertices. Such points are called **triangle centers**. There is a standard list of triangle centers, each labeled by an index. The $n$-th triangle center is denoted $\X_n$.

(1) The **incenter** $I$ is one of the fixed points of the isogonal conjugation, labeled $\X_1$. Let the anticevian triangle of $I$ be $I_AI_BI_C$, then $I_A$ is the $A$-**excenter**, and define the $B,C$-excenters similarly. The triangle $I_AI_BI_C$ is called the **excentral triangle**.

(2) The **medial triangle** of $ABC$ is the triangle with vertices the midpoints of $BC,CA,AB$. The medial triangle and $ABC$ are perspective, with perspector the tripole $G$ of $\ell_\infty$. The point $G$ is called the **centroid**, labeled $\X_2$.

(3) The center $O$ of $\odot(ABC)$ is called the **circumcenter**, labeled $\X_3$.

(4) The isogonal conjugate $H$ of the circumcenter is called the **orthocenter**, labeled $\X_4$.

(5) The isogonal conjugate $K$ of the centroid is called the **symmedian point**, labeled $\X_6$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
On the complex projective plane, we cannot define the incenter to be the fixed point in the "interior" of $ABC$, so we arbitrarily pick one as the incenter, and the others are called excenters.
:::

:::{#lem-orthocenter}
Let the orthocenter of $ABC$ be $H$, then $AH\perp BC$ (this is where the orthocenter got its name).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Let the circumcenter be $O$, and let $AO$ intersect the circumcircle at $A'$. We have
$$
\sangle(AH,BC)=\sangle HAB\cdot\sangle ABC=\sangle CAA'\cdot \sangle ABC=\sangle CBA'\cdot \sangle ABC=\sangle ABA'
$$
Since $\sangle ABA'=(A,A';\infty_+,\infty_-)_{\odot(ABC)}=-1$ (from @lem-harmonicquad), $AH\perp BC$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let the incenter and excentral triangle be $I,I_AI_BI_C$, then $AI,AI_B$ are the fixed lines of the isogonal conjugation on $\mathbb{L}_A$, so $A(I,I_B;\infty_+,\infty_-)=-1$, i.e. $AI\perp AI_B$. From @lem-orthocenter, $I$ is the orthocenter of $I_AI_BI_C$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
The circumconic of the symmedian point $K$ is $\odot(ABC)$. This follows from @lem-isoconjline and the fact that the image of $\ell_\infty$ under the isogonal conjugation is $\odot(ABC)$. From @lem-trilineardual, the tripolar of any point on the circumcircle passes through $K$.
:::

## Foci of Conics and Optical Properties

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic. Consider the two tangents $m_1,m_2$ (resp. $n_1,n_2$) of $\mathcal{C}$ through $\infty_+$ (resp. $\infty_-$). Set $m_i\cap n_j=F_{ij}$ for $i,j=1,2$. We call $F_{ij}$ the **foci** of $\mathcal{C}$, and $(F_{11},F_{22})$ is called a pair of foci, and $(F_{12},F_{21})$ is the other pair. By Brocard theorem and polarity, the midpoint of a pair of foci is the center of the conic. All four foci of a circle coincide at its center.
:::

:::{#lem-focusproperty}
## optical property
Let $F_{11},F_{22}$ be a pair of foci of the conic $\mathcal{C}$. For a point $P$, let $\ell_1,\ell_2$ be the two tangents of $\mathcal{C}$ through $P$, then $\sangle (F_{11}P,\ell_1)=\sangle(\ell_2,F_{22}P)$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Consider the tangents $\infty_+F_{11},\infty_+F_{22},\infty_-F_{11},\infty_-F_{22}$ of $\mathcal{C}$. Apply DDIT to this quadrilateral and the point $P$, 
$$
(\ell_1,\ell_2),\, (PF_{11},PF_{22}),\, (P\infty_+,P\infty_-)
$$
is an involution, so
$$
\sangle (F_{11}P,\ell_1)=(\infty_{F_{11}P},\infty_{\ell_1};\infty_+,\infty_-)=(PF_{11},\ell_1;P\infty_+,P\infty_-)=(PF_{22},\ell_2;P\infty_-,P\infty_+)
$$
We similarly see that $\sangle (F_{11}P,\ell_1)=\sangle(\ell_2,F_{22}P)$.
:::

:::{#cor-focusisogonal}
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be an inconic (i.e. a conic tangent to the three sides) of $ABC$, $F_{11},F_{22}$ be a pair of foci of $\mathcal{C}$, then $F_{11}$, $F_{22}$ are isogonal conjugates with respect to $ABC$.
:::

:::{#lem-focusconicexist}
Given a pair of isogonal conjugates $P,Q$, then there exists a unique inconic of $ABC$ with $P,Q$ a pair of foci.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
It suffices to prove that there exists a conic tangent to the lines
$$
BC,\,CA,\,AB,\,P\infty_+,\,P\infty_-,\,Q\infty_+,\, Q\infty_-
$$
(the uniqueness is clear). Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a conic tangent to $AB,P\infty_+,P\infty_-,\,Q\infty_+,\, Q\infty_-$, and the other tangent from $A$ to $\mathcal{C}$ be $\ell$. Apply DDIT to $P\infty_+,P\infty_-,Q\infty_+, Q\infty_-\in \mathcal{T}_\mathcal{C}$ and the point $A$,
$$
(AB,\ell),\,(AP,AQ),\,(A\infty_+,A\infty_-)
$$
is an involution. This is an isogonal involution on $\mathbb{L}_A$, so $\ell=AC$. Similarly, $AC$ and $BC$ are both tangent to $\mathcal{C}$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
We define the **angle bisectors** of $\sangle BAC$ to be the fixed lines of the involution $(AB,AC),(A\infty_+,A\infty_-)$ (the lines passing through $A$ such that $\sangle(AB,\ell)=\sangle(\ell,AC)$). We know that the two angle bisectors are perpendicular.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
Let the cevian triangle of the orthocenter $H$ of $ABC$ be $H_aH_bH_c$. Since $AH\perp BC$ and $H_a(A,B;H_b,H_c)=-1$, $AH$ and $BC$ are the angle bisectors of $\sangle H_bH_aH_c$.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
Applying @lem-focusproperty to the case $P\in \mathcal{C}$, we see that the tangent of $P$ is an angle bisector of $\sangle F_{11}PF_{22}$. This shows that the definition of foci coincides with the classical definition.
:::

:::{#lem-four-incircles}
Given a triangle $ABC$, there exists exactly $4$ circles tangent to the three sides of $ABC$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $\omega$ is a circle tangent to the three sides of $ABC$ with center $I$, then from @lem-focusproperty, $I$ is the isogonal conjugate of itself, so $I$ must be one of the four fixed points of the isogonal conjugation. From @lem-focusconicexist, there exists a unique conic with focus $I,I$ that is tangent to the three sides of $ABC$. As there are four fixed points, there are four such circles.
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
Among the four circles tangent to the three sides, the one centered at the incenter is called the **incircle**, and the one centered at the $A$-excenter is called the $A$-**excircle**. Analogously define the $B,C$-excircles.
:::

Writing the circular points of infinity out: given $ABC$, there exists exactly four inconics of $ABC$ that pass through $\infty_+,\infty_-$. Since the circular points of infinity are arbitrary points, we obtain the following.

:::{#cor-five-elements-conics}
Five points and lines in total determine finitely many conics:

(1) Given five points (no three are collinear), there exists a unique conic through these five points.

(2) Given four points $A,B,C,D$ (no three are collinear) and a line $\ell$ not passing through these points, then there exist exactly two conics passing through $A,B,C,D$ and tangent to $\ell$. 

(3) Given three points $P,Q,R$ and two lines $m,n$ not passing through $P,Q,R$ such that no three of $P,Q,R,m\cap n$ are collinear, there exist exactly four conics passing through $P,Q,R$ and tangent to $m,n$.

The cases "$3$ lines and $2$ points", "$4$ lines and $1$ point", and "$5$ lines" are the dual of the previous cases, which determine $4,2,1$ conics, respectively. 
:::

:::{#lem-tangent-quad-focus}
Let $F$ be a focus of the conic $\mathcal{C}$, lines $AB,BC,CD,DA$ are tangent to $\mathcal{C}$, then $\sangle AFB=\sangle DFC$.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Apply DDIT to $AB,BC,CD,DA\in \mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{C}}$ and the point $F$,
$$
(F\infty_+,F\infty_-), \,(FA,FC), \,(FB,FD)
$$
is an involution, so $\sangle AFB=\sangle DFC$.
:::

Replacing the four tangents with two pairs of coinciding tangents (i.e. two tangents at $P\in \mathcal{C}$ and two tangents at $Q\in \mathcal{C}$), we obtain the following.

:::{#cor-pole-bisector}
Let $F$ be a focus of $\mathcal{C}$ and $P,Q$ be two points on $\mathcal{C}$. Suppose that $R$ is the pole of $PQ$, then $FR$ is an angle bisector of $\sangle PFQ$.
:::

## Circumconics, Inconics, and the Symmedian Point

Let $ABC$ be a triangle, the circumconic and inconic of $P$ be $\mathcal{C}_1,\,\mathcal{C}_2$, respectively, then $\mathfrak{p}_{\mathcal{C}_2}(P)$ is the tripolar of $P$. Let $\mathcal{C}_2$ intersect the tripolar of $P$ at $Q,R$, then $PQ$ and $PR$ are tangents of $\mathcal{C}$. Taking the $P$-anticomplement, $\mathcal{C}_1$ passes through $Q,\,R$, and $PQ,\,PR$ are tangents, too, so $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ are tangent at $Q,R$.

:::{#lem-thirdrootofunitypoints}
Let the tripole $\ell$ of $P$ with respect to $ABC$ intersect the circumconic $\mathcal{C}_1$ of $P$ at $Q,R$, then $R$ is on the tripolar of $Q$ (similarly, $Q$ is on tripolar of $R$).
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
The image of $\ell$ under the isoconjugation $P\times P$ is $\mathcal{C}_1$, so $P\times P$ swaps $Q$ and $R$.

Given $X\in \mathcal{C}_1$, let $Y$ be the intersection of the tripolar of $X$ and $\ell$, $Z=P\times P\div Y\in \mathcal{C}_1$. Consider the projective map
$$
f:\mathcal{C}_1\to \mathcal{C}_1,\,X\mapsto Z
$$
Let $AP$ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ intersect again at $A'$, then $f(A)=A'$. Similarly we see that $f$ is the involution with perspector $P$, i.e. $f(Q)=Q$. We conclude that $P\times P\div Q=R$ is the intersection of the tripolar of $Q$ and $\ell$. 
:::

From @lem-trilineardual, the circumconic and tripolar of $Q$ intersect at $P,R$, so the relation between the three points are symmetric.

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
$P,Q,R$三點滿足
$$
P\times P=Q\times R,\,Q\times Q=R\times P,\,R\times R=P\times Q
$$
:::

:::{#lem-3-inv}
令$P$對$ABC$的外接錐線與內切錐線為$\mathcal{C}_1$與$\mathcal{C}_2$，
$$
f:\mathcal{C}_1\to\mathcal{C}_1\,\text{保交比},\,f(A)=B,\, f(B)=C,\, f(C)=A
$$
則對所有$X\in\mathcal{C}_1$，$Xf(X)$切$\mathcal{C}_2$。
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
注意到$f$的射影軸為$P$的三線性極線，故$f$的不動點為$P$的三線性極線與$\mathcal{C}_1$的交點$Q,\,R$。由@lem-autenvelope ，$Xf(X)$的軌跡為一錐點，且此錐點包含
$$
Af(A)=AB,\,Bf(B)=BC,\,Cf(C)=CA,\,Qf(Q)=QP,\,Rf(R)=RP
$$
這五線都與$\mathcal{C}_2$相切，故$Xf(X)$切$\mathcal{C}_2$對於$X\in \mathcal{C}_1$。
:::

現在考慮類似重心$K$的外接錐線$\odot(ABC)$與內切錐線$\mathcal{C}$。由@lem-3-inv ，令$f:\odot(ABC)\to \odot(ABC)$使$f(A)=B,\,f(B)=C,\,f(C)=A$，則$\infty_+,\infty_-$對$\mathcal{C}$的切線為
$$
\infty_+f(\infty_+),\,\infty_+f^{-1}(\infty_+),\, \infty_-f(\infty_-),\,\infty_-f^{-1}(\infty_-)
$$
以下考慮$\mathcal{C}$的其中一對焦點$\infty_+f(\infty_+)\cap\infty_-f^{-1}(\infty_-),\,\infty_+f^{-1}(\infty_+)\cap\infty_-f(\infty_-)$。

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Definition**
三角形$ABC$的布洛卡點$Br,Br'$滿足
$$
\sangle BrAB=\sangle BrBC=\sangle BrCA,\,\sangle Br'BA=\sangle Br'CB=\sangle Br'AC
$$
因為$\odot(BrBC)$與$CA$相切，對稱地，兩布洛卡點都是唯一的，且互為等角共軛。
:::

接下來的目標是證明類似重心的內切錐線$\mathcal{C}$的一對焦點為兩布洛卡點。

:::{#lem-brocardpoint}
給定$ABC$，$\mathcal{C}$為$ABC$的一外接錐線，
$$
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\,\text{保交比},\,f(A)=B,\, f(B)=C,\, f(C)=A
$$
$X,Y$為$\mathcal{C}$上任意兩點，$Xf(X)\cap Yf(Y)=Z$，則$(XYZAB)$與$AC$相切。
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
相切等價$A(C,Z;Y,B)=X(A,Z;Y,B)$。令$AZ$交$\mathcal{C}$於$W$，則等價證明
$$
(C,W;Y,B)_{\mathcal{C}}\,\text{與}\,(A,f(X);Y,B)_{\mathcal{C}}=(f(X),A;B,Y)_{\mathcal{C}}
$$
相同，也就是要證明$Cf(X)$, $WA$, $BY$共點(對合)，這等價
$$
Cf(X)\cap BY,\,A,\, Xf(X)\cap Yf(Y)\,\text{共線}
$$
注意到$(Y,X;C,A)=(f(Y),f(X);A,B)=(f(X),f(Y);B,A)$。也就是存在
$$
g:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}\,\text{保交比},\,g(Y)=f(X),\, g(X)=f(Y),\, g(C)=B,\, g(A)=A
$$
考慮$g$的射影軸$\ell$，可知$\ell$上有$Cf(X)\cap BY$, $A$, $Xf(X)\cap Yf(Y)$三點，這就是前面等價要證明的三點共線。
:::

:::{#cor-brocardpointinconic}
令$f:\odot(ABC)\to\odot(ABC)\,
\text{保交比},\,f(A)=B,\, f(B)=C,\, f(C)=A$，則布洛卡點$Br'=\infty_+f(\infty_+)\cap \infty_-f(\infty_-),\,Br=\infty_+f^{-1}(\infty_+)\cap \infty_-f^{-1}(\infty_-)$為類似重心的內切錐線之一對焦點 (由@lem-brocardpoint 中$X=\infty_+,\,Y=\infty_-$得到)。
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
@lem-brocardpoint 可以令$X,Y$為動點使用大保交比證明，也就是把無窮虛圓點當成外接圓上的動點來操作。
:::

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Example**
令外心為$O$，$\odot(ABC)$與類似重心$K$的內切錐線$\mathcal{C}$相切於$Q,R$兩點，則有$O,K,Br,Br',Q,R$共圓$\omega$，稱為布洛卡圓。這是因為

1. 令$X$為$\odot(ABC)$上的一點，$X$對$\odot(ABC)$的切線為$\ell$，$X$對$\mathcal{C}$的切線為$m,n$。對$Q,Q,R,R$對$\odot(ABC),\,\mathcal{C}$的四切線以及$X$使用DDIT(對兩錐線分別用)，可知
$$
(XK,XK),\,(XQ,XR),\,(\ell,\ell),(m,n)
$$
為對合，故$(\ell,XK;m,n)=-1$。取$X=\infty_\pm$，則
$$
\infty_+(O,K;Br,Br')=\infty_-(O,K;Br,Br')=-1
$$
2. 考慮保交比的$f:\odot(ABC)\to \odot(ABC),\,f(A)=B,\,f(B)=C,\,f(C)=A$，其不動點為$Q,R$，由@lem-fixcrossratio ，$(X,f(X);Q,R)_{\odot(ABC)}=c$的值與$X\in \odot(ABC)$無關。取$X=\infty_+$，有
$$
\infty_+(O,Br';Q,R)=(\infty_+,f(\infty_+);Q,R)_{\odot(ABC)}=c
$$
對稱地$\infty_+(O,Br';Q,R)=\infty_-(O,Br';Q,R)=c$，$\infty_+(O,Br;Q,R)=\infty_-(O,Br;Q,R)$。

綜合以上可知$O,K,Br,Br',Q,R$共圓(因為$K,Q,R$不共線)。
:::

這是一個不用算角度證明共圓的例子。

:::{.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**
因為$O\infty_+,O\infty_-,KQ,KR$為$\odot(ABC)$的切線，
$$
(O,K;\infty_+,\infty_-)_\omega=Q(O,K;\infty_+,\infty_-)=-1\text{，同理 }(O,K;Q,R)_\omega=-1
$$
故$\omega$的中心在$OK$上。結合$(O,K;Br,Br')_\omega=-1$可知$BrBr'\perp OK\perp QR$。
:::
